g.title: 📌 Wright's failure branch. Regressing to a defensive Chain is the other option, and it is the one that disintegrates.
📌 The problem does not get easier by itself. Somebody standardised it. This edge is the whole argument.
📌 An unwritten, untaught practice lowers D for nobody.
📌 D is high relative to B. Wright's chart says a Team here is the WORST of the three, and a Team that picks wrong is a mob.
📌 The only composition whose strength does not depend on D. When you cannot honestly calibrate how hard the problem is, this is the safe default.
📌 One member's success. Still an anecdote — it is not yet a process, and it does not yet lower D for anybody else.
📌 Marc's gloss on Wright, and the load-bearing move: naming, writing and teaching what the Pack found. This is the ONLY lever that lowers D.
📌 Now that the work is specifiable it can be handed off. Every link costs ln N, so build the shortest chain that does the job.
📌 Consensus is now the strongest composition, because D has fallen below the group's average B. Team-work is a REWARD for having made the problem easy.
📌 The empirical test of whether the problem is still easy. A process in control is the signature of a D that has stayed down.
📌 D has risen again, or B has fallen. The group is no longer entitled to Team-work and must go back out as a Pack.
📌 See One, Do One, Teach One is the other half of the scissors. Standardising lowers D; teaching raises B. Both move the same gap, and teaching is how a standard process actually propagates.
